question: What must many states require before a person can operate a three-wheel motorcycle?
choice_a: A separate license or endorsement, requiring the rider to pass both a written and a skills test
choice_b: No additional license is ever required beyond a Class M endorsement
choice_c: Only a skills test, with no written component
explanation: Many states require a separate license or endorsement to operate a three-wheel motorcycle, requiring the rider to pass both a written and a skills test.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.49, 'Three-Wheel Supplement'

question: What is the maximum turning diameter, at its widest point, for a vehicle to generally be considered a three-wheel motorcycle under the characteristics described?
choice_c: There is no turning diameter limit
explanation: Among the general characteristics of a three-wheel motorcycle, the turning diameter of the vehicle at its widest point must be less than 40 feet.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.49, 'Know Your Vehicle'

question: Where must a passenger be seated on a three-wheel motorcycle designed for a passenger, per the general characteristics described?
choice_a: In front of the operator at all times
choice_b: Standing on a running board beside the operator
choice_c: Behind the operator, or in a separate passenger compartment in the case of a motorcycle with a sidecar
explanation: If designed for a passenger, the passenger must be seated behind the operator, or in a separate passenger compartment in the case of a motorcycle with a sidecar.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.49, 'Know Your Vehicle'

question: What is the difference between "dual track" and "triple track" three-wheel motorcycle designs?
choice_a: There is no distinction; the terms are interchangeable
choice_b: Dual track always means two rear wheels and no sidecar
choice_c: Triple track refers only to vehicles with four wheels
choice_d: Dual track vehicles are motorcycles with sidecars, while triple track motorcycles are configured with dual front or dual rear wheels
explanation: Unlike traditional single-track motorcycles, three-wheel motorcycles could be either dual or triple track design -- dual track vehicles are motorcycles with sidecars, while triple track motorcycles can be configured with dual front wheels or dual rear wheels.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.49-50, 'Three-Wheel Motorcycle Designs'

question: Why do conventional three-wheel motorcycles steer differently from two-wheel motorcycles?
choice_a: Because they cannot lean, they cannot countersteer -- instead, the front wheel is pointed directly in the direction the rider wants to go
choice_b: They use exactly the same countersteering technique as a two-wheel motorcycle
choice_c: Three-wheel motorcycles have no steering mechanism at all
choice_d: They steer only through body-weight shifting, never through the handlebars
explanation: Because conventional three-wheel motorcycles cannot lean, they cannot countersteer; instead, the front wheel is pointed in the direction the rider wants the motorcycle to go.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.51, 'Steering & Tip-Over'

question: What are "tip-over lines," and why do they matter for load and passenger positioning?
choice_a: They are painted lines on the roadway that three-wheel motorcycles must never cross
choice_b: They mark the boundary beyond which enough weight transfer can lift a wheel off the road during turning or tight maneuvers, so loads and passengers must be kept within them for stability
choice_c: They only apply to two-wheel motorcycles
choice_d: They have no effect on vehicle stability
explanation: Under some conditions, it is possible for a three-wheel motorcycle to have only two wheels in contact with the road, which can occur during turning or tight maneuvers when enough weight is transferred outside the tip-over lines -- careful load and passenger positioning within these lines helps maintain maximum stability.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.51, 'Body Position'

question: On a motorcycle with a sidecar, what can happen to the sidecar wheel during braking in a sharp turn?
choice_a: The sidecar wheel automatically locks to prevent lifting
choice_b: Sidecars are unaffected by braking forces during turns
choice_c: The sidecar wheel may lift off the ground
choice_d: The motorcycle's front wheel lifts instead
explanation: On a motorcycle with a sidecar, during braking in a sharp turn, the sidecar wheel may lift off the ground, since traction is greater when the motorcycle is rolling rather than skidding or slipping.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.51-52, 'Braking'

question: During a right turn on a motorcycle with a sidecar, what tends to happen, especially if the sidecar is empty or lightly loaded?
choice_a: The sidecar wheel is pressed more firmly into the road
choice_b: Right turns behave identically to left turns in every case
choice_c: The sidecar detaches automatically for safety
choice_d: A slight sideways movement of the center of gravity creates a greater tendency for the sidecar wheel to lift
explanation: During a right turn, a slight sideways movement of the center of gravity creates a greater tendency for the sidecar wheel to lift; the lift will be greater if the sidecar is empty or lightly loaded.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.52, 'Turning'

question: When turning left on a motorcycle with a sidecar, why does the sidecar act as a stabilizer keeping its wheel on the ground?
choice_a: During a left-hand turn, the sidecar acts as a stabilizer so its wheel stays on the ground, unless the turn is too sharp or too fast, which can lift the motorcycle's rear wheel instead
choice_b: The sidecar wheel always lifts during every left turn regardless of speed
choice_c: Left and right turns behave identically on a sidecar rig
choice_d: The sidecar has no influence on turning behavior
explanation: During a left-hand turn, the sidecar acts as a stabilizer so the sidecar wheel stays on the ground; however, if the turn is taken too sharply or at too high a speed, the rear suspension may extend and the rear wheel of the motorcycle may lift off the ground.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53, 'Turning'

question: What should a rider do when turning left on a motorcycle with a sidecar?
choice_a: Accelerate hard into the turn for stability
choice_b: Reduce speed prior to entering the turn and apply more pressure on the rear brake than on the front
choice_c: Apply only the front brake and avoid the rear brake entirely
choice_d: Steering technique is identical to a right turn
explanation: When turning left on a motorcycle with sidecar: reduce speed prior to entering the turn, and apply more pressure on the rear brake than on the front.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53, 'Turning'

question: What happens to traction on the front tire(s) when riding uphill on a three-wheel motorcycle or motorcycle with a sidecar?
choice_b: Uphill grades have no effect on weight distribution
choice_c: Weight shifts to the rear, making the front lighter and reducing front-tire traction for steering and grip
choice_d: Weight shifts entirely to the sidecar wheel
explanation: When riding uphill, some weight will shift to the rear, causing the front of the motorcycle to become lighter; this weight shift reduces the traction on the front tire(s) for steering and tire grip.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53, 'Hills'

question: Why should a rider begin slowing earlier for cornering and stopping when riding downhill on a three-wheel motorcycle?
choice_a: Downhill braking requires less force than on level ground
choice_b: Gravity has no effect on braking requirements
choice_c: Braking is only a concern on uphill grades
choice_d: Gravity increases the amount of braking force required to slow or stop the motorcycle
explanation: When riding downhill, gravity increases the amount of braking force required to slow or stop the motorcycle, so it is important to begin slowing earlier for cornering and stopping.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53, 'Hills'

question: Why is a rider's lane positioning limited on a three-wheel motorcycle or motorcycle with sidecar compared to a two-wheel motorcycle?
choice_a: The track of the dual wheels is almost as wide as some automobiles, so the rider must keep toward the center of the lane to avoid crossing painted lines
choice_b: Three-wheel motorcycles are exempt from all lane positioning rules
choice_c: Lane position is identical to a two-wheel motorcycle in every respect
choice_d: Riding at the far right edge of the lane is always safest
explanation: The track of the dual wheels of a three-wheel motorcycle or motorcycle with sidecar is almost the same width as some automobiles; keep toward the center of the lane to be sure the dual wheels don't cross the painted lines into opposing traffic or leave the pavement on the right.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53, 'Lane Position'

question: Can a group of three-wheel motorcycles use a staggered formation like two-wheel motorcycles?
choice_a: Yes, staggered formation works identically for three-wheel motorcycles
choice_b: No -- lane positioning limitations mean a staggered formation cannot be used; ride single file with at least a two-second margin
choice_c: Group riding rules do not apply to three-wheel motorcycles
choice_d: Three-wheel motorcycles must always ride two abreast
explanation: You will not be able to use a staggered formation, as you would when riding two-wheeled motorcycles; ride single file and always maintain a safe margin, two seconds minimum, between vehicles.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.53-54, 'Lane Position'

question: If braking is required while swerving on a three-wheel motorcycle or motorcycle with sidecar, when should the rider brake?
choice_a: Only while actively swerving, for maximum control
choice_b: Braking and swerving should always happen at the exact same instant
choice_c: Either before or after the swerve, never while swerving
choice_d: Braking is unnecessary since three-wheel vehicles cannot skid
explanation: A three-wheel motorcycle or motorcycle with sidecar is not as maneuverable as a two-wheel motorcycle, so plan well ahead to avoid sudden turns; if braking is required, brake either before or after the swerve, never while swerving.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.54, 'Swerving'

question: On a motorcycle with a sidecar carrying only one passenger, where should that passenger sit, and why?
choice_a: Always on the saddle behind the rider, regardless of the sidecar
choice_b: Passenger placement makes no difference to stability
choice_c: Standing on the sidecar's running board
choice_d: In the sidecar -- never on the saddle alone, since the added weight on the tip-over line would increase instability
explanation: On a motorcycle with a sidecar, the best place for a single passenger is in the sidecar; never put a single passenger on the saddle, since the added weight on the tip-over line will increase the instability of the motorcycle.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.54-55, 'Carrying Passengers and Cargo'

question: During acceleration on a motorcycle with a sidecar, what tendency does the added off-centered weight of the sidecar create, and how should a rider compensate?
choice_a: The vehicle feels as though it is being steered to the right; compensate by steering slightly in the opposite direction from the sidecar
choice_b: The vehicle feels as though it is being steered to the left during acceleration
choice_c: Acceleration has no directional effect with a sidecar attached
choice_d: Compensation should always be made by braking, never steering
explanation: During acceleration, the sidecar's non-powered, off-centered mass lags behind, making the motorcycle feel as though it is being steered to the right; compensate by steering slightly in the opposite direction from the sidecar.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.54, 'Acceleration and Deceleration'
